missions.title: Eco Market
missions.subtitle: Read the clues and help the shops
missions.guide: Read every clue. Choose the message that is accurate and useful.
missions.reminder: Remember: A passive sentence focuses on the thing receiving an action. Enough means the amount meets a need.

tasks.prompt: Every morning, workers wash the glass bottles. Choose the correct passive sentence about the bottles.
options: The glass bottles are washed every morning.
The glass bottles is washed every morning.
The glass bottles are wash every morning.
tasks.answer: The glass bottles are washed every morning.
tasks.full: The glass bottles are washed every morning.
tasks.hint: Bottles is plural. Use are followed by the past participle washed.
tasks.explain: Are washed focuses on the bottles that receive the action. Use are with a plural noun and washed after are.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 passive voice

tasks.prompt: Workers make bags from old shirts and notebooks from old paper. A notice swaps the two materials. Which edit corrects both product-and-material relationships?
options: The bags are made from old paper, and the notebooks are made from old shirts.
The bags are made from old shirts, and the notebooks are made from old paper.
The bags are made from old shirts, and the notebooks are made from old shirts.
tasks.answer: The bags are made from old shirts, and the notebooks are made from old paper.
tasks.full: The bags are made from old shirts, and the notebooks are made from old paper.
tasks.hint: Check each finished product separately. Bags use shirts; notebooks use paper. Both parts of the edit must be correct.
tasks.explain: The edit restores both relationships: shirts become bags, and paper becomes notebooks. Are made from focuses on each product and names its material.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 passive voice
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil separates two material-to-product relationships, detects the swapped references and selects an edit that restores both; every option uses the same correct passive form.

tasks.prompt: A pie needs at least five apples. Box A has three, Box B has five and Box C has eight. Choose the smallest amount that is enough, without taking extra apples.
options: Choose Box C because it has more apples than Box B.
Choose Box A because it has fewer apples than Box B.
Choose Box B because it has enough apples without any extra.
tasks.answer: Choose Box B because it has enough apples without any extra.
tasks.full: Choose Box B because it has enough apples without any extra.
tasks.hint: Check both conditions: at least five apples, and no extra apples.
tasks.explain: A has too few apples. C has enough but includes three extra. B meets both conditions with exactly five apples.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 comparisons with too and not enough; recycled comparisons
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil evaluates three choices against a minimum quantity and a no-waste condition, then selects the reasoned recommendation; the grammar is correct in every option.

tasks.prompt: Seven visitors each need one cup. Tray A has eight cups and Tray B has six. Which note explains why the shop should use Tray A?
options: Tray B does not have enough cups, but Tray A does.
Both trays have enough cups for all seven visitors.
Tray A does not have enough cups, but Tray B does.
tasks.answer: Tray B does not have enough cups, but Tray A does.
tasks.full: Tray B does not have enough cups, but Tray A does.
tasks.hint: Compare each tray with seven visitors. Your note must describe both trays accurately.
tasks.explain: Six cups are not enough for seven people, while eight cups are enough. The contrast supports using Tray A.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 comparisons with not enough; recycled conjunctions
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil relates two quantities to a shared need and tests both parts of a contrasting statement; recalling the phrase enough cups does not identify the correct note.

tasks.prompt: A paper bag becomes weak in the rain. A plastic bag stays strong when wet. It is raining now. Which packing note uses the evidence to protect the shopping?
options: The shopping is packed in the paper bag because it stays strong when wet.
The shopping is packed in the plastic bag because it stays strong when wet.
The shopping is packed in the paper bag because there is no rain.
tasks.answer: The shopping is packed in the plastic bag because it stays strong when wet.
tasks.full: The shopping is packed in the plastic bag because it stays strong when wet.
tasks.hint: Match the bag material to the weather and check the reason after because.
tasks.explain: The plastic bag stays strong in the given wet conditions. The passive note describes a choice supported by the material and weather clues.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 passive voice; recycled conjunction because
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil evaluates a practical choice using material properties and current weather, rejecting notes with an unsupported reason despite their grammatical form.

missions.title: Message Bridge
missions.subtitle: Keep people and messages clear
missions.topic: Reported speech · question tags · reference pronouns
missions.guide: Choose a message that keeps the facts, speakers and grammar correct.
missions.reminder: Remember: Check who is speaking and who each pronoun means. A question tag checks a statement: can't ... , can ...?

tasks.prompt: Complete the question that checks this positive statement: You carry a map, ___?
options: don't you
do you
isn't you
tasks.answer: don't you
tasks.full: You carry a map, don't you?
tasks.hint: A positive present simple statement takes a negative tag with do.
tasks.explain: Carry is a present simple verb. The positive statement You carry a map takes the negative question tag don't you.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 question tags

tasks.prompt: Sara said, "I am ready." Report her words later, changing am to its past form.
options: Sara said she were ready.
Sara said she was ready.
Sara said she be ready.
tasks.answer: Sara said she was ready.
tasks.full: Sara said she was ready.
tasks.hint: I becomes she when you report Sara's words. The past form of am with she is was.
tasks.explain: The report uses she for Sara and was as the past form of am. This task practises the requested past-form report.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 reported speech

tasks.prompt: Ali told Sara, "I have your map." Later, Sara tells Mina who had her map. Which is Sara's accurate report, using the past form had?
options: Ali said Sara had his map.
Sara said she had Ali's map.
Ali said he had my map.
tasks.answer: Ali said he had my map.
tasks.full: Ali said he had my map.
tasks.hint: Ali spoke first, so he refers to Ali. Sara is now speaking, so her own map is my map.
tasks.explain: Ali is the original speaker and map holder. In Sara's report, he refers to Ali and my refers to Sara, the map owner.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 reported speech; recycled reference pronouns
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil tracks the original speaker, current speaker and owner through a change of viewpoint; every option uses had, so tense recall alone is insufficient.

tasks.prompt: Mina and her brother borrowed a boat together. Only her brother returned it. Mina's draft says, "We borrowed the boat and we returned it." Which edit fixes who did the second action?
options: We borrowed the boat, but he returned it.
He borrowed the boat, but we returned it.
We borrowed the boat, but she returned it.
tasks.answer: We borrowed the boat, but he returned it.
tasks.full: We borrowed the boat, but he returned it.
tasks.hint: We includes Mina and her brother. The second action was done by only one person: her brother.
tasks.explain: We correctly describes the two borrowers. He identifies the brother as the only person who returned the boat, and it refers to the boat.
tasks.dskpTopic: Recycled reference pronouns and conjunctions
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil compares a draft against two different sets of actors, locates the inaccurate reference and chooses an edit that preserves both events.

tasks.prompt: The keeper says, "Visitors can enter only before six." It is now six thirty. Which checking question follows the rule and uses the correct question tag?
options: We can enter now, can't we?
We can't enter now, can we?
We can enter until seven, can't we?
tasks.answer: We can't enter now, can we?
tasks.full: We can't enter now, can we?
tasks.hint: First decide whether entry is allowed at six thirty. Then use a positive tag after the negative statement.
tasks.explain: Six thirty is after the entry deadline, so We can't enter now follows the rule. The negative statement takes the positive tag can we.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 question tags; recycled can for permission
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil applies a time restriction to the present situation, derives the permission statement and checks tag polarity; all three offered questions have grammatical tags.

missions.title: Experience Train
missions.subtitle: Build questions about experience and time
missions.topic: Present perfect · ever · for · since · How long?
missions.guide: Put the carriages in order. Check have or has and the past participle.
missions.reminder: Remember: Use have or has with a past participle. For gives a length of time; since gives the starting point.

tasks.prompt: Ask whether your friend has visited Sabah at any time before now. Start with Have and end with Sabah?
tasks.answer: Have you ever visited Sabah?
tasks.full: Have you ever visited Sabah?
tasks.hint: Put Have before you. Ever comes before the past participle visited.
tasks.explain: Have you ever visited asks about an experience at any time up to now, without naming a finished past date.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 present perfect with ever

tasks.prompt: Hana began living here in 2022 and still lives here. Build a sentence with since. Start with Hana and end with 2022.
tasks.answer: Hana has lived here since 2022.
tasks.full: Hana has lived here since 2022.
tasks.hint: Use has with Hana. Since introduces the starting year.
tasks.explain: Has lived connects Hana's past starting point with the present. Since 2022 gives the starting point.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 present perfect with since

tasks.prompt: Build a sentence saying that we began living here three years ago and still live here. Use for. Start with We and end with years.
tasks.answer: We have lived here for three years.
tasks.full: We have lived here for three years.
tasks.hint: Use have with we. For introduces the length of time: three years.
tasks.explain: Have lived describes a situation that continues now. For three years tells us its duration.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 present perfect with for

tasks.prompt: Ask about the length of Amin's stay at the camp, which is still continuing. Start with How and end with camp?
tasks.answer: How long has Amin stayed at the camp?
tasks.full: How long has Amin stayed at the camp?
tasks.hint: Start with How long. Put has before Amin, then use the past participle stayed.
tasks.explain: How long asks for a duration. Has Amin stayed uses present perfect for a stay that continues now.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 present perfect with How long

tasks.prompt: Ask whether he has eaten dragon fruit at any time before now. Start with Has and end with fruit?
tasks.answer: Has he ever eaten dragon fruit?
tasks.full: Has he ever eaten dragon fruit?
tasks.hint: Use has with he. The past participle of eat is eaten.
tasks.explain: Has he ever eaten asks about an experience. Eaten is the past participle used after has.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 present perfect with ever

missions.title: River Timeline
missions.subtitle: Build a story about past actions
missions.topic: Past continuous with past simple · used to
missions.guide: Put the blocks in order. Show the action in progress and the event that happened.
missions.reminder: Remember: Was or were plus an ing verb shows a past action in progress. Used to describes a past habit or situation.

tasks.prompt: He began reading before the bell rang and was still reading at that moment. Start with He and end with rang.
tasks.answer: He was reading when the bell rang.
tasks.full: He was reading when the bell rang.
tasks.hint: Use was reading for the action in progress. When introduces the shorter event.
tasks.explain: Was reading is past continuous. The past simple rang names the event during that action.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 past continuous with past simple

tasks.prompt: They were on a walk when the rain began. Build the sentence. Start with They and end with rain.
tasks.answer: They were walking when it started to rain.
tasks.full: They were walking when it started to rain.
tasks.hint: Use were with they. Were walking is the action already in progress.
tasks.explain: Were walking describes the continuing past action. Started describes when the rain began during the walk.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 past continuous with past simple

tasks.prompt: We played in this park regularly in the past, but we do not play here now. Start with We and end with here.
tasks.answer: We used to play here.
tasks.full: We used to play here.
tasks.hint: Use used to before the base verb play for the past habit.
tasks.explain: Used to play describes the former routine. The prompt tells us this routine no longer continues.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 used to

tasks.prompt: She was a farmer before she became a teacher. Describe the former situation with used to. Start with She and end with farmer.
tasks.answer: She used to be a farmer.
tasks.full: She used to be a farmer.
tasks.hint: Used to is followed by a base verb. Here, use be.
tasks.explain: Used to be describes her former situation. The prompt tells us her job has changed.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 used to

tasks.prompt: The cat escaped during Tom's sleep. Build the sentence with While. Start with While and end with escaped.
tasks.answer: While Tom was sleeping, the cat escaped.
tasks.full: While Tom was sleeping, the cat escaped.
tasks.hint: While introduces the action in progress: Tom was sleeping. Put a comma before the main event.
tasks.explain: Was sleeping is the background action. Escaped is the past simple event that happened during it.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 past continuous with past simple

missions.title: Evidence Mine
missions.subtitle: Separate evidence from a guess
missions.guide: Read the evidence. Choose a careful message that does not claim more than we know.
missions.reminder: Remember: May, might and could can show a possibility. Nobody and nothing mean no person and no thing.

tasks.prompt: The basket is completely empty. Complete the sentence: There is ___ in the basket.
options: nothing
someone
everything
tasks.answer: nothing
tasks.full: There is nothing in the basket.
tasks.hint: An empty basket contains no things. Choose the pronoun that means no thing.
tasks.explain: Nothing means no thing. It fits the information that the basket is empty.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 indefinite pronouns

tasks.prompt: We hear a sound in the cave. It could be an animal or the wind. We have not looked inside. Which message uses the evidence carefully?
options: An animal is definitely inside the cave.
There cannot be an animal inside the cave.
An animal may be inside the cave, but we are not sure.
tasks.answer: An animal may be inside the cave, but we are not sure.
tasks.full: An animal may be inside the cave, but we are not sure.
tasks.hint: A sound gives a possibility, but there are two possible causes. Avoid a claim of certainty.
tasks.explain: May shows a possibility. The sound could come from an animal or the wind, so the evidence does not prove either cause.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 modal verbs for speculation
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil compares competing explanations with incomplete evidence and selects an appropriately uncertain claim; every option is a grammatical sentence.

tasks.prompt: All three bags have been checked. The key is not in any bag. The table has not been checked. Which report separates a known fact from a possibility?
options: The key isn't in any bag, and it isn't on the table.
We can't find the key in any bag, but it might be on the table.
The key is in a bag, but it might be on the table.
tasks.answer: We can't find the key in any bag, but it might be on the table.
tasks.full: We can't find the key in any bag, but it might be on the table.
tasks.hint: The bag search is complete. The table is still unknown, so use a possibility for the table.
tasks.explain: The first part reports the completed search. Might be on the table is only a possibility because nobody has checked the table.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 modal verbs for speculation and indefinite pronouns
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil distinguishes checked locations from an unchecked location, then tests a two-part statement for the correct degree of certainty in each part.

tasks.prompt: After heavy rain, the hut floor is wet and its window is open. Which possible explanation is supported by both clues?
options: The floor might be wet because sunshine came through the window.
The floor might be wet because the window was closed throughout the rain.
The floor might be wet because rain came through the open window.
tasks.answer: The floor might be wet because rain came through the open window.
tasks.full: The floor might be wet because rain came through the open window.
tasks.hint: Connect the wet weather to the open window. Use might because the clues support an explanation without proving it.
tasks.explain: Rain and an open window together support this possible cause of the wet floor. Might keeps the explanation cautious.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 modal verbs for speculation; recycled because and past simple
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil connects weather, an opening and a wet floor to infer a plausible cause, while retaining uncertainty; all options contain the same correct modal form.

tasks.prompt: Four children enter the mine. Only Nora and Amir carry lamps. Siti and Jun have none. No child has a map. Which edit fixes this draft: "Everyone has a lamp, and someone has a map"?
options: Everyone has a lamp, but nobody has a map.
Some children have lamps, and someone has a map.
Some children have lamps, but nobody has a map.
tasks.answer: Some children have lamps, but nobody has a map.
tasks.full: Some children have lamps, but nobody has a map.
tasks.hint: Only two of the four children have lamps. Check the map statement separately.
tasks.explain: Some accurately describes two of the four children. Nobody correctly reports that no child has a map. Both errors in the draft are fixed.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 indefinite pronouns; recycled conjunctions and quantities
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil checks two separate claims against a four-person set, detects both overgeneralisation and a false existence claim, and selects the only edit that fixes both.

missions.title: Decision Portal
missions.subtitle: Make a future plan from the clues
missions.guide: Choose the future message that fits every time, rule and plan clue.
missions.reminder: Remember: In a first conditional, use present simple after if and will plus a base verb for the result. Timetables can use present simple.

tasks.prompt: Tomorrow's timetable says 9:00 am. Complete the timetable sentence: The train ___ at nine tomorrow morning.
options: left
leaves
leaving
tasks.answer: leaves
tasks.full: The train leaves at nine tomorrow morning.
tasks.hint: A fixed timetable can use present simple even when the event is tomorrow.
tasks.explain: Leaves is present simple with the singular subject train. Present simple is used for this scheduled future event.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 present simple for future events

tasks.prompt: The race uses the field on dry days. On rainy days, it uses the hall only if the hall is open. Tomorrow the hall is closed. Which plan follows both rules if it rains?
options: If it rains, we will hold the race another day.
If it rains, we will hold the race on the field.
If it rains, we will hold the race in the hall.
tasks.answer: If it rains, we will hold the race another day.
tasks.full: If it rains, we will hold the race another day.
tasks.hint: Rain rules out the field. The hall is allowed only when it is open, so check that restriction too.
tasks.explain: Rain rules out the field, and the closed hall rules out the indoor choice. Holding the race another day follows both restrictions. If it rains uses present simple, followed by will hold for the result.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 first conditional
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil combines a weather rule with a separate hall-opening restriction, eliminates both immediate places and chooses a feasible future outcome; every option has a grammatical first conditional.

tasks.prompt: The museum opens at ten and stays open all afternoon. Our bus reaches the stop at nine forty-five. The walk takes twenty minutes. Which entry plan is possible?
options: We are going to enter the museum before ten.
We are going to enter the museum at nine forty-five.
We are going to enter the museum after ten.
tasks.answer: We are going to enter the museum after ten.
tasks.full: We are going to enter the museum after ten.
tasks.hint: Add the walk to the bus arrival time, then compare that time with the opening time.
tasks.explain: Nine forty-five plus twenty minutes is ten oh five. The museum is open then, so the plan to enter after ten fits all the times.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 future forms: going to; present simple for future events
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil calculates an arrival time and tests it against an opening constraint to choose a feasible plan; all options use the same correct going to structure.

tasks.prompt: The club starts at four. From the bus stop, the walk takes twenty minutes. Bus A arrives at three fifty; Bus B arrives at three thirty. Which promise follows from the times?
options: If we take Bus A, we will arrive before the club starts.
If we take Bus B, we will arrive before the club starts.
If we take Bus B, we will miss the start of the club.
tasks.answer: If we take Bus B, we will arrive before the club starts.
tasks.full: If we take Bus B, we will arrive before the club starts.
tasks.hint: Work out each arrival at the club, including the walk. Compare both with four o'clock.
tasks.explain: Bus A gives an arrival of four ten, which is late. Bus B gives three fifty, so its conditional promise is supported by the times.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 first conditional; present simple for future events
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil combines travel stages for two alternatives and checks the predicted outcome of each conditional rather than selecting a verb form by recall.

tasks.prompt: The gardener has bought seeds and made a firm plan to plant them tomorrow. The forecast says rain is possible, but not certain. Which note clearly states the plan and keeps the weather uncertain?
options: He is going to plant seeds tomorrow, but it might rain.
He might plant seeds tomorrow, and it is certain to rain.
He is going to plant seeds tomorrow, and it cannot rain.
tasks.answer: He is going to plant seeds tomorrow, but it might rain.
tasks.full: He is going to plant seeds tomorrow, but it might rain.
tasks.hint: Use going to for the firm plan. Use a possibility word for the uncertain weather.
tasks.explain: Is going to plant reports the planned action. Might rain respects the forecast's uncertainty and does not claim that rain is certain or impossible.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 future forms and modal verbs for speculation
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil evaluates the certainty of two different pieces of information and selects a message that treats the planned action and uncertain forecast appropriately.

missions.title: Rescue Rules
missions.subtitle: Choose advice with a clear reason
missions.topic: should · must · have to · do not have to
missions.guide: Check the rules and the evidence. Choose accurate advice for the rescue team.
missions.reminder: Remember: Should gives advice. Must and have to can show an obligation. Do not have to means something is not required.

tasks.prompt: Choose the grammatically correct advice for a child who needs help with a difficult task.
options: You should to ask an adult for help.
You should ask an adult for help.
You should asks an adult for help.
tasks.answer: You should ask an adult for help.
tasks.full: You should ask an adult for help.
tasks.hint: Put a base verb directly after should, without to or s.
tasks.explain: Should gives advice and is followed directly by the base verb ask.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 modal verbs for advice

tasks.prompt: Wearing a helmet is a camp rule. Complete the sentence: Mina ___ to wear a helmet.
options: have
having
has
tasks.answer: has
tasks.full: Mina has to wear a helmet.
tasks.hint: Use has with one person, Mina. Has to shows that the rule requires it.
tasks.explain: Has to expresses an obligation. The singular subject Mina takes has.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 modal expressions for obligation: have to

tasks.prompt: The sign says: "Helmets are required. Gloves are optional." Which message explains both rules accurately?
options: You don't have to wear a helmet, but you must wear gloves.
You must wear a helmet, but you don't have to wear gloves.
You must wear a helmet, and you must wear gloves.
tasks.answer: You must wear a helmet, but you don't have to wear gloves.
tasks.full: You must wear a helmet, but you don't have to wear gloves.
tasks.hint: Required means an obligation. Optional means you may choose, so it is not required.
tasks.explain: Must wear a helmet expresses the required action. Don't have to wear gloves means gloves are optional; it does not forbid them.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 modal verbs for obligation
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil distinguishes a compulsory item from an optional item and checks both clauses against the sign; every option uses grammatical obligation expressions.

tasks.prompt: Ravi's water bottle is empty. Station A has drinking water and is five minutes away, but it is closed until tomorrow. Station B also has drinking water, is forty-five minutes away and is open now. Which advice fits his need and the opening times?
options: You should fill your bottle at Station A because it is closer.
You should skip both stations because your bottle is full.
You should fill your bottle at Station B because it is open now.
tasks.answer: You should fill your bottle at Station B because it is open now.
tasks.full: You should fill your bottle at Station B because it is open now.
tasks.hint: A shorter journey helps only if the station can provide water now. Check whether each place is open.
tasks.explain: Ravi needs water now. A is closer but closed; B is open. B is therefore the usable place in the stated choices, and the reason correctly explains that decision.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 modal verbs for advice; recycled comparisons and because
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil identifies the need, weighs distance against availability and rejects the tempting nearer but closed option; each option uses the same correct should structure.

tasks.prompt: The rescue hall rule says everyone must keep quiet. The cat hides when it hears loud sounds. Amir suggests blowing a whistle; Lina suggests waiting calmly. Which message respects the rule and the cat's behaviour?
options: We must keep the hall quiet, so we should blow the whistle.
We must keep the hall quiet, so we should wait calmly.
We don't have to keep the hall quiet, so we should shout.
tasks.answer: We must keep the hall quiet, so we should wait calmly.
tasks.full: We must keep the hall quiet, so we should wait calmly.
tasks.hint: Test each action against the quiet rule and the cat's reaction to loud sounds.
tasks.explain: Waiting calmly keeps the hall quiet and avoids the loud sounds that make the cat hide. Must states the rule; should recommends the suitable action.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 modal verbs for obligation and advice; recycled so
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil evaluates two proposed actions against both an external rule and behavioural evidence, choosing a recommendation with a consistent reason.

missions.title: Castle Evidence
missions.subtitle: Use more than one comparison clue
missions.topic: as ... as · enough · comparative and superlative forms
missions.guide: Look at the objects and read all the clues. Tap the one that fits.
missions.reminder: Remember: As tall as means the same height. For a reasoning challenge, one matching clue is not enough: check every condition.

tasks.prompt: Tower A and Tower B have the same height. Choose the other tower that is as tall as Tower A.
tasks.answer: b
tasks.full: Tower B is as tall as Tower A.
tasks.hint: As tall as means equal in height. The instruction asks for a tower other than A.
tasks.explain: Tower B and Tower A have the same height. Tower C is taller, so B matches as tall as A.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 comparisons with as, too and not enough; recycled comparative and superlative forms

tasks.prompt: Choose the tallest of these three towers.
tasks.answer: c
tasks.full: Tower C is the tallest of the three towers.
tasks.hint: The tallest tower is higher than every other tower in the group.
tasks.explain: Tower C is higher than A and B, so the superlative tallest identifies C.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 comparisons with as, too and not enough; recycled comparative and superlative forms

tasks.prompt: Choose the chest that is smaller than Chest A.
tasks.answer: b
tasks.full: Chest B is smaller than Chest A.
tasks.hint: Compare the two chests. Smaller means less big than the other one.
tasks.explain: Chest B is less big than Chest A. Smaller is the comparative form of small.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 comparisons with as, too and not enough; recycled comparative and superlative forms

tasks.prompt: Chest A holds four gems, B holds eight and C holds twelve. The team has seven gems. Choose the smallest chest that is big enough for all seven.
tasks.answer: b
tasks.full: Chest B is big enough for seven gems and smaller than Chest C.
tasks.hint: First reject a chest that cannot hold seven gems. Then choose the smaller of the chests that can.
tasks.explain: A is not big enough. B and C can hold seven gems, but B is smaller, so it meets both conditions.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 comparisons with as, too and not enough; recycled comparative and superlative forms
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil eliminates an insufficient option, compares the remaining sufficient options and chooses the smallest feasible one; identifying the biggest or smallest alone fails.

tasks.prompt: The key is in a tower taller than both A and C, but not as tall as D. Choose the only tower that fits all three comparisons.
tasks.answer: b
tasks.full: Tower B is taller than A and C, but it is not as tall as D.
tasks.hint: Check taller than A, taller than C, and shorter than D separately. The answer must pass all three checks.
tasks.explain: B is taller than both A and C and shorter than D. D fails the last condition, and A and C fail a taller-than condition.
tasks.dskpTopic: Year 6 comparisons with as, too and not enough; recycled comparative and superlative forms
tasks.kbatRationale: The pupil combines three comparative relationships, rules out different distractors for different reasons and finds the one object satisfying the complete set of constraints.

rules: shop
Passive voice and enough
is / are + past participle · enough + noun · adjective + enough
A passive sentence focuses on the thing receiving the action. Enough means a need is met; not enough means it is not met.
The bags are made from old shirts. This tray has enough cups.
bridge
Reports and checking questions
said + reported message · positive statement, negative tag?
In a past-form report, check pronouns and the changed verb. Question tags check understanding; match the tag to the statement.
Sara said she was ready. You carry a map, don't you? We can't enter, can we?
train
Experience and duration
have / has + past participle · ever · for / since · How long?
Ever asks about experience up to now. For gives a length of time. Since gives a starting point. How long asks for duration.
Have you ever visited Sabah? Hana has lived here since 2022.
boat
Past actions and former habits
was / were + verb-ing + when + past event · used to + base verb
Past continuous describes a past action in progress. Past simple can name an event during it. Used to describes a past habit or situation.
He was reading when the bell rang. She used to be a farmer.
pickaxe
Possibility and careful evidence
may / might / could + base verb · someone / nobody / nothing
A possibility is not a proven fact. Check which places or people are known, and which are still unknown. Nobody means no person; nothing means no thing.
The key might be on the table. Nobody has checked it yet.
portal
Conditions and future plans
If + present simple, will + base verb · be going to · timetable present simple
Match a condition to its correct result. Going to can describe a plan. A fixed future timetable can use present simple.
If it rains, we will use the hall. The train leaves at nine tomorrow.
cat
Rules and reasoned advice
should + base verb · must + base verb · have / has to · do not have to
Should gives advice. Must and have to can express an obligation. Do not have to means not required. A good reason must match the evidence.
You must wear a helmet, but you don't have to wear gloves.
castle
Comparison decisions
as tall as · taller than · the tallest · big enough
As ... as compares equal qualities. A comparative relates things; a superlative gives an extreme in a group. Check every condition before choosing.
Chest B is big enough for seven gems and smaller than Chest C.

curriculum.note: Original Year 6 SK grammar activities for a higher-ability class. Topic boundaries follow the Year 6 grammar list and permitted recycling of earlier primary grammar. The challenge comes from connected clues, evidence, editing and decisions. These short tasks practise supporting language; they do not assess the full longer-text, interaction or two-paragraph learning standards, and game scores are not a PBD performance level.
curriculum.kbatDefinition: The KPM/BPK Year 6 DSKP, printed page 12, describes HOTS as using knowledge, skills and values for reasoning, reflection, problem solving and decisions, across applying, analysing, evaluating and creating. Here, a KBAT item requires a contextual inference or a decision against multiple facts or criteria; a direct form-recall, guided word-order or single comparison item is not counted. The task-level cognitiveLevel and kbatRationale record that distinction.
